userPrompt: Can I require employees to work more than 48 hours a week in the EU?
responseText:
**No, not as a blanket requirement.**

In the EU, the **Working Time Directive (2003/88/EC)** sets a hard limit:

- **Maximum average working time**: 48 hours per week, including overtime, averaged over a reference period (usually 4 months, up to 6 or 12 months in some cases depending on national law).
- This is a mandatory rule in all EU member states. You cannot impose a contractual term or policy that systematically requires employees to work more than 48 hours on average.

### Key practical points:
- **Opt-out possibility**: Most member states allow **individual opt-outs** (the employee must agree in writing, voluntarily, and can revoke it). Even with an opt-out, you must still monitor health & safety, record hours, and respect daily/weekly rest rules (11 consecutive hours daily rest, 24/48 hours weekly rest).
- Some countries (e.g. France, Spain, Belgium) have stricter rules or make opt-outs difficult in practice.
- **No forced overtime beyond the cap**: You cannot discipline, dismiss, or disadvantage an employee for refusing to exceed the 48-hour average or for revoking an opt-out.
- Certain sectors (transport, healthcare, etc.) and senior management (“workers whose working time is not measured or predetermined”) may be partially or fully exempt.

**Recommendation**:  
Never write “employees must work up to X hours” if X > 48. Instead, set normal hours (e.g. 37.5–40) and regulate overtime with clear limits, opt-out forms where allowed, and proper records.

National rules differ (e.g. UK post-Brexit still follows the 48-hour rule but with easier opt-outs). Always check the specific member state’s transposition of the Directive and consult local employment counsel before implementing any policy.
